name: Kailash & Tibet (via Nepal)
tagline: Kailash yatra and Tibet tours from Nepal
meta_description: Kailash Mansarovar yatra via Nepal by Kerung, Simikot heli or Lhasa, plus Lhasa and Everest north tours. INR prices, seasons, permits and Indian rules.
summary: Our Kailash and Tibet trips start in Nepal. The Kailash Mansarovar yatra takes 9–17 days by road via Kerung, by flight and helicopter via Simikot and Hilsa, or by air via Lhasa, from about ₹2,10,000 per person. The season runs from May to September, and the parikrama crosses Dolma La at about 5,630 m.
intro: Mount Kailash, 6,638 m, stands alone on the plateau of western Tibet about 100 km north of Nepal's border at Hilsa. Hindus revere it as the abode of Shiva, Buddhists as the home of Demchok, Jains as Ashtapad, and Bon followers as the soul of their faith. Nobody climbs it. Pilgrims walk the 52 km parikrama from Darchen instead, over three days, and bathe in Lake Manasarovar at about 4,590 m. Nepal is the most practical starting point for a private yatra, with three routes and departures through the summer.

The overland route drives from Kathmandu across the Rasuwagadhi–Kyirong border, acclimatises in Kyirong at about 2,700 m and crosses the plateau via Saga to the lake, about 14 days in all. The Simikot route flies Kathmandu–Nepalgunj–Simikot, takes a 20–30 minute helicopter hop to Hilsa and drives through Purang, which cuts the trip to 11 or 12 days. The Lhasa route flies in, adds three days among the city's monasteries and drives west for four days. The Kerung crossing was closed by floods in August 2026; check current status before you travel.

Every route is high. Saga sits at about 4,640 m, Darchen at 4,575 m and Dirapuk, the first night of the parikrama, at about 4,900 m, before Dolma La at about 5,630 m. Itineraries therefore build in nights at Kyirong or Purang and two nights at Manasarovar before the walk. Ponies and porters are hired through the Darchen cooperative, and pilgrims who cannot walk the circuit can still visit the lake and Tarboche for darshan on our 9-day yatra without the parikrama.

Tibet beyond Kailash is open to tours too. Lhasa, at 3,656 m and about 75–90 minutes by air from Kathmandu, has the Potala Palace, the Jokhang and the Barkhor; Gyantse and Shigatse follow on the road west, and Rongbuk looks up at the north face of Everest. All travel in Tibet is in groups on a Chinese group visa with a licensed Tibetan guide, and the rules for Indian passport holders have changed in most seasons since 2023, so we confirm them in writing before every booking.

highlights.title: The parikrama over Dolma La
highlights.text: The outer kora around Kailash is about 52 km from Darchen, usually walked in three days with nights at Dirapuk and Zuthulpuk. Day two climbs past Shiva Sthal to Dolma La at about 5,630 m, then drops past Gauri Kund in a long day of 8–10 hours. Eco-buses cut the walking to about 42–45 km.

highlights.title: Holy dip at Lake Manasarovar
highlights.text: Manasarovar, at about 4,590 m, covers some 410 km² below Gurla Mandhata. Pilgrims drive the 90–100 km shore road, stop at ghats for puja and havan, take a dip or a bucket snan and fill bottles of water to carry home. Most groups sleep two nights by the lake, facing Kailash across the plain.

highlights.title: Kailash north face at Dirapuk
highlights.text: The first night of the parikrama is spent at Dirapuk, at about 4,900 m, where the north face of Kailash rises sheer above the guesthouses across the Lha Chu valley. At sunrise the face turns gold, the view most pilgrims remember longest. A small gompa built around an old meditation cave stands on the slope opposite.

highlights.title: Saga Dawa at Tarboche
highlights.text: On the full moon of the fourth Tibetan month, usually late May or June, thousands of pilgrims gather at Tarboche, on the first stretch of the kora, to watch the great prayer-flag pole lowered, re-dressed and raised. Our one Saga Dawa departure a year is timed to reach Darchen for the ceremony.

highlights.title: Lhasa's Potala and Jokhang
highlights.text: Lhasa, at 3,656 m, is 75–90 minutes by air from Kathmandu. The 13-storey Potala Palace, the Jokhang temple with the Barkhor pilgrim circuit around it, and the monk debates at Sera fill three days, which also help the body adapt before any drive west. Short tours of 5–8 days run in most months.

highlights.title: Everest from the north at Rongbuk
highlights.text: Rongbuk, at about 4,980 m, is the end of the road below Everest's north face, with a monastery and the viewpoint for the north base camp at about 5,150–5,200 m. It is reached from Shigatse over the Pang La in a long day, as part of our 10-day Lhasa to Kathmandu overland trip.

getting_there: There are three ways from Nepal to Kailash. Overland, drive about 165 km from Kathmandu to the Rasuwagadhi–Kyirong border in 7–9 hours, then continue via Saga to Lake Manasarovar over three more travel days with acclimatisation stops. By air and helicopter, fly Kathmandu–Nepalgunj in an hour, Nepalgunj–Simikot in 40–50 minutes, and take a 20–30 minute helicopter hop to Hilsa; from there you walk across the bridge and drive through Purang to the lake. Pilgrims from Lucknow can instead drive to Nepalgunj via Rupaidiha in 4–5 hours. The third option is to fly Kathmandu–Lhasa in 75–90 minutes and drive west for four days. The Kerung crossing closed after floods in August 2026; check current status before you travel.
permits: All foreign visitors, Indians included, need a Chinese group visa issued to the whole group, a Tibet Travel Permit, an Alien's Travel Permit for Ngari and the military and frontier permits that Kailash requires. A licensed Tibetan agency applies for them about 3–4 weeks ahead, and you must stay with your group and guide throughout Tibet. In recent seasons resident Indians have had visas processed through the Chinese embassy in New Delhi with original passports and biometrics, an age limit near 70 has applied, and NRIs have travelled in separate groups. On the Simikot route your operator also handles Nepal-side formalities in Humla. Check current status before you travel.

months.weather: Lhasa −9 to 8 °C, dry and sunny; Darchen below −20 °C at night
months.summary: January is closed season at Kailash. Darchen and Manasarovar lie under snow and ice, guesthouses on the parikrama shut, and permits for Ngari are not issued to pilgrim groups. Lhasa is a different matter: days are sunny and dry, and Tibetan pilgrims from the countryside crowd the Barkhor and the Jokhang in winter. Short Lhasa tours can run while Tibet Travel Permits are being issued, but foreign travel usually closes around Losar in February or March.
months.tip: Pack for nights near −10 °C even in Lhasa, because hotel heating is uneven in winter.

months.weather: Lhasa −6 to 10 °C, dry with strong winds; Shigatse −9 to 9 °C
months.summary: February is usually the quietest month for foreign travel in Tibet. Losar, the Tibetan New Year, falls in February or early March, and in most recent years the authorities have stopped issuing Tibet Travel Permits to foreign visitors from around Losar until early April. Kailash is deep in winter, with Darchen at −15 °C or colder at night. Use these weeks to plan: choose a route, gather documents and book a summer yatra departure.
months.tip: Indian pilgrims should start passport and medical paperwork in February for a May or June yatra.

months.summary: March is usually closed to foreign tourists in Tibet, with permits reopening in late March or April depending on the year. Lhasa warms slowly and the first group tours return once permits are issued. Kailash remains snowbound, and the routes from Kyirong and Hilsa are not yet open to pilgrims. This is the main booking window for the season: fixed departures for May, June and Saga Dawa fill first, and the visa process for Indian pilgrims needs weeks of lead time.
months.tip: Book Saga Dawa departures by March, because seats on the Simikot flights and rooms in Darchen sell out first.

months.summary: April reopens Tibet for most foreign travellers, usually from early or mid-month. Lhasa, Gyantse and Shigatse are dry and quiet, with clear skies and cold nights, and the road to Rongbuk opens for Everest north-face trips, which are at their clearest in April and May. Kailash permits are usually not yet available to pilgrims; the first yatra groups cross the border in May. A Lhasa tour this month is a good way to see Tibet before the summer groups.
months.tip: Confirm that Tibet permits are being issued before booking an early-April Lhasa flight.

months.weather: Darchen −3 to 12 °C; Purang 3 to 18 °C, mostly dry
months.summary: May opens the Kailash yatra season. The first groups cross at Kyirong and Hilsa in early to mid May, roads across the plateau are dry and skies are mostly clear, though snow can still lie on Dolma La and nights at Dirapuk fall well below freezing. Crowds are smaller than in June. Saga Dawa falls in late May in some years, bringing thousands of Tibetan pilgrims to Tarboche. Lhasa, Gyantse and Rongbuk are also in good season.
months.tip: Book a pony for day two in May, as snow on Dolma La can be icy at dawn.

months.weather: Darchen 3 to 16 °C; Manasarovar 2 to 15 °C, mostly dry
months.summary: June is the busiest month at Kailash and one of the most comfortable. Days are mild, the plateau greens at the edges and Manasarovar is usually calm in the mornings. Indian groups arrive in large numbers, so guesthouses at Dirapuk and Zuthulpuk fill and Darchen is busy. Saga Dawa often falls in June. On the Nepal side, pre-monsoon cloud starts to delay Nepalgunj–Simikot flights in the second half of the month, so build in a spare day.
months.tip: Ask your operator to book ponies and porters before arrival in June, when demand at the Darchen cooperative peaks.

months.weather: Darchen 6 to 17 °C, afternoon showers; Lhasa 10 to 23 °C
months.summary: July brings the monsoon to Nepal, which affects the journey more than Kailash itself. The plateau gets only light afternoon showers, and Kailash and Manasarovar are often clear in the mornings, but landslides can block the road to Rasuwagadhi and cloud delays Simikot flights. Guru Purnima, the full moon usually in July, draws many Indian pilgrims to Manasarovar for puja. Lhasa is at its warmest and greenest, with long evenings.
months.tip: Allow two spare days in July whichever route you take, because monsoon delays on the Nepal side are common.

months.weather: Manasarovar 5 to 16 °C, occasional rain; Lhasa 9 to 21 °C
months.summary: August is much like July: the plateau is mild and fairly dry while the Nepal side is wet. Many Indian groups travel during Shravan, the month sacred to Shiva. In August 2026 floods closed the Rasuwagadhi–Kyirong crossing again, so overland yatras moved to the Simikot and Lhasa routes; check current status before you travel. In Lhasa, Shoton opens with a giant thangka unveiled at Drepung Monastery, usually in August, followed by Tibetan opera in the Norbulingka.
months.tip: Book Lhasa hotels early for Shoton, one of the city's busiest weeks of the year.

months.summary: September is the second peak of the yatra season and, for many pilgrims, the best. The monsoon ends in Nepal through the month, Simikot flights become more reliable, skies over the plateau are at their clearest and crowds are lighter than in June. Nights grow colder quickly: by late September Dirapuk drops well below freezing and fresh snow can dust Dolma La. Shoton sometimes falls in early September in Lhasa.
months.tip: Choose a departure in the first half of September if you want milder nights on the parikrama.

months.weather: Darchen −6 to 9 °C; Lhasa 1 to 17 °C, dry and clear
months.summary: October closes the Kailash season. The last yatra groups usually return by early or mid October, when snow and nights near −10 °C on Dolma La end the parikrama and services in Darchen wind down. Central Tibet, by contrast, is in excellent shape: Lhasa, Gyantse and Shigatse are dry and clear, and Rongbuk gives some of the sharpest views of Everest's north face. China's national holiday week at the start of the month brings domestic crowds to Lhasa.
months.tip: Avoid 1–7 October for Lhasa, when the holiday week fills hotels and Potala entry slots.

months.weather: Lhasa −5 to 12 °C, dry and sunny; Gyantse −10 to 9 °C
months.summary: November is off-season at Kailash; Ngari is cold and the pilgrim routes are closed. Lhasa tours still run, with lower prices, empty monasteries and long sunny days, though nights fall well below freezing. Roads to Gyantse and Shigatse stay open, and Rongbuk is possible early in the month in dry years. Choose a well-heated hotel in Lhasa and keep the itinerary short, with a rest day on arrival.
months.tip: Bring lip balm and moisturiser for Lhasa in November, because the air is extremely dry.

months.weather: Lhasa −8 to 8 °C, sunny and dry; Shigatse −10 to 7 °C
months.summary: December is quiet in Tibet. Kailash and Manasarovar are frozen and closed to pilgrims, and the road west of Saga carries little traffic. Lhasa remains open to tours in most years, and winter is when nomads and farmers make their own pilgrimages to the Jokhang, so the Barkhor fills with Tibetan pilgrims rather than tourists. It is also the time to plan the next yatra and start passport and medical paperwork.
months.tip: Check Tibet permit status before booking December flights, because closures can be announced at short notice.

faqs.q: How much does the Kailash Mansarovar Yatra cost from Nepal?
faqs.a: Our yatras start from about ₹2,10,000 per person for 14 days overland via Kerung, ₹2,95,000 for 11 days via Simikot and Hilsa by helicopter, and ₹3,25,000 for 16 days with a Lhasa fly-in, twin sharing. A private helicopter charter starts from about ₹3,85,000. Ponies, porters, the visa fee, insurance and tips are usually extra.

faqs.q: Can Indian passport holders do the Kailash yatra via Nepal?
faqs.a: Yes, through a Nepali agency working with a licensed Tibetan agency. In recent seasons resident Indians have needed to submit original passports at the Chinese embassy in New Delhi weeks before departure, give biometrics, carry a medical certificate and, for 2026, be born in 1955 or later. NRIs have travelled in separate groups. These rules change most years; check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: What is the best time for the Kailash Mansarovar Yatra?
faqs.a: May, June and September. The season runs from about early May to early October, with departures through July and August, when Nepal's monsoon can delay flights and roads. June is busiest; September is clearest and less crowded. Saga Dawa, usually late May or June, is the most auspicious time for Buddhists. Kailash is closed to pilgrims from mid-October to April.

faqs.q: How many days does the Kailash yatra take from Nepal?
faqs.a: Between 9 and 17 days. Via Simikot and Hilsa by helicopter it takes 11 days from Kathmandu; from Lucknow via Nepalgunj, 12 days; overland via Kerung, 14 days; with a Lhasa fly-in, 16 days; and our slower senior-pilgrim itinerary takes 17. A Manasarovar trip without the parikrama takes 9 days. Shorter itineraries skip acclimatisation and are not safe.

faqs.q: Is there an age limit for the Kailash yatra via Nepal?
faqs.a: In recent seasons a limit near 70 has applied to Indian passport holders, expressed for 2026 as birth year 1955 or later, with occasional conditional exceptions. A medical certificate is required. Other nationalities have faced fewer age rules but the same altitude. Whatever the rule, your doctor should approve travel above 5,000 m. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How difficult is the Kailash parikrama?
faqs.a: It is a strenuous high-altitude walk, not a technical climb. After the eco-bus sections, about 42–45 km remain over three days, and the hardest day crosses Dolma La at about 5,630 m in 8–10 hours. Most fit pilgrims manage with good acclimatisation, a slow pace and a pony for day two. Mild headache is common; worsening symptoms mean turning back.

faqs.q: Which is better for Kailash, the Kerung or Simikot route?
faqs.a: Kerung, by road, is cheaper, avoids flight risk and acclimatises gradually over about 14 days, but it depends on the Rasuwagadhi border, which closed after floods in August 2026. Simikot saves about three days and long drives, but costs more and relies on the weather for small-plane and helicopter flights. Seniors often prefer Simikot for less road time. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Can I do the Kailash yatra by helicopter?
faqs.a: Partly. Helicopters fly only on the Nepal side, from Simikot to Hilsa in 20–30 minutes or by private charter from Nepalgunj. Inside Tibet all travel is by road, and helicopters do not land at Manasarovar or on the parikrama. Separately, Shree Airlines has run Kailash darshan flights from Nepalgunj that view the mountain without landing; check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Can I visit Lhasa from Kathmandu?
faqs.a: Yes. Flights from Kathmandu to Lhasa take about 75–90 minutes, and you need a Chinese group visa and a Tibet Travel Permit, both arranged by a licensed agency. Our Lhasa tours run 5–8 days from about ₹98,000 per person, and a 10-day trip continues to Everest's north side. Most foreign tours pause from around February to early April.
